agent-pipeline <version> run <runId> · <duration>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)
  noted    #8 comment · from #3 implement · the CLI help drifts from the README
  handed   #5 Fix Stage with a single retry · verify · 1 unmet
  noted    #31 new · from #5 fix · nothing cleans up abandoned worktrees
  skipped  #7 no-criteria
  skipped  #9 blocked

Frontier empty.

The verb is padded to nine columns so the Ticket numbers line up. A Run that
took no Ticket prints `  nothing to do` in place of the rows.

`<version>` is the Version the Run ran (ADR-0007): the number alone from an
installed copy, and the number, the commit and a `dirty` mark from a development
checkout — `0.4.0`, `0.4.0+331d79c`, `0.4.0+331d79c.dirty`. Every stamp of one
Run says the same thing, and `.agent-pipeline/runs/<runId>/version.txt` says it
again beside the transcripts.

A Run whose Version is below the highest one published on GitHub gains a line
above that header, which is also the first thing it logged hours earlier:

A newer Version is out: 0.5.0, and this is 0.4.0 — upgrade with `npm install -g "github:jjongs2/agent-pipeline#semver:*"`.
agent-pipeline <version> run <runId> · <duration>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)

Frontier empty.

Nothing is printed where this copy is the latest Version, where it is above it —
a development checkout runs a commit past the Version it reports, and is
compared by number only — or where GitHub could not be asked at all. No answer
is an answer, and none of them stops a Run.

The rows are in the order the Tickets ended, which is the order they were
claimed in only for a Run with one Lane. A Run with more than one has several
Tickets in flight at once, and each takes as long as its own Stages take.

`released` is a Ticket the subscription rate limit stopped mid-flight: its Claim
was undone, and the State file it has been keeping since it was claimed says
where the next Run resumes it from. Nobody has to do anything about it, which is
why it is not `handed`. It stops the Run filling Lanes, so no Ticket is claimed
after it; the Lanes still busy finish what they hold, and whatever they end as
has its row after the `released` one:

agent-pipeline <version> run <runId> · <duration>

  released #6 Rebase conflict resolution · rate limit at implement
  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)

Rate limited.

A Ticket a Run resumed has no row of its own, released or stranded: it merges,
is handed off, or is released again like any other, and the header already names
the Run that took it.

`skipped` names why a candidate was passed over: `blocked` for one an open
blocker held back all Run, and otherwise the guard reason that kept it from
being claimed — `spec`, `no-criteria` or `body-only-blockers` for Planning a
guard rejected, `claimed` or `not-ready` for an issue that is nobody's to take,
which is usually one `ticket <n>` named by hand. A stranded Ticket is not one of
those: it wears this checkout's own Claim, so it is resumed rather than `skipped`
as `claimed`.

`noted` is a Note a Stage made, and follows the row of the Ticket whose Stage
made it. Its number is where the Note went, not where it came from: `comment`
for a Note that reached an issue already there — the Ticket it named, or a
standing Notes issue already open — and `new` for the one Note of a Run that
found no standing Notes issue and opened it. Most of a Run's Notes land on the
same number as `comment`, which is what gathering them on one issue means. The
row shows the Note's summary trimmed to one line; the whole Note is on GitHub.

The last line says why the Run stopped: `Frontier empty.` when nothing is left,
`Frontier blocked.` when every remaining candidate has an open blocker,
`Rate limited.` when a Release ended the Run, and `Stopped at <hh:mm> · ...`
when a human stopped it.

A Run the limit stopped prints no `skipped  #<n> blocked` rows and no rows for
the Frontier Tickets it never reached: it stopped before it could say a
candidate was held back all Run. The rows its Lanes earned and the last line are
the whole report.

The `blocked` rows of any other Run are read off the last Frontier it computed,
which is the one its final refill asked for. A candidate another Lane unblocked
on the way was taken rather than held back, so it is not among them.

A Run a human stopped takes no further Ticket, and the Lanes busy when the Stop
arrived finish what they hold. Its last line names the clock time the Stop
arrived and the Tickets those Lanes were holding, so the rows above it can be
read as everything the Run had left to do:

agent-pipeline <version> run <runId> · <duration>

  merged   #3 Run: drain the Frontier (PR #12)
  merged   #6 Rebase conflict resolution (PR #14)

Stopped at 22:07 · finishing #3 #6.

The time is UTC to the minute, which is the clock the run id in the header is
already written in. A Run with no Lane busy when the Stop arrived has nothing to
finish and says so:

Stopped at 22:07 · nothing to finish.

Like a Run the limit stopped, a stopped Run prints no `skipped  #<n> blocked`
rows and no rows for the Tickets it never reached: it stopped before it could
say a candidate was held back all Run. A Stop that reaches a Run a Release had
already stopped leaves the last line `Rate limited.`, because that is what
stopped it; the Stop only asked for what was already happening.

`ticket <n>` prints the same header and its one row, and stops there: it drains
no Frontier, so it says nothing about one — a Stop included. It takes one Ticket
whatever happens, so a Stop asks it for nothing it was not already doing, and
the line it logs when the Stop arrives is the whole of what it says about one.
